group.passage: On many bags of coffee, shoppers find a small label saying that the beans were traded fairly. Behind that label lies a long-standing worry. Most of the world’s coffee is grown on small family farms, and the price these farmers receive can rise and fall sharply from one year to the next. In October 2001, for example, the world price sank to a record low of 45 cents a pound, bringing hardship to small growers across the developing world. Fair trade is designed to soften such shocks. To use the label, buyers must purchase coffee from farmers who are organized into cooperatives, groups run democratically by their members. Buyers must also pay at least a minimum price, which is based on the estimated cost of growing coffee in a sustainable way. When the market price is higher than this floor, the higher price applies instead. In addition, buyers agree to long-term trading relationships and, if asked, pay part of the money in advance. The deal also includes a small extra sum known as the premium. It is meant for the group as a whole rather than for any single farmer, and members vote on how to spend it. Common choices include training, services for members, quality programs, and community projects. During the 2001 crisis, the system proved its worth: the price paid for fair-trade coffee was 180 percent higher than the market price. When world prices are high, however, the advantage shrinks, and some farmers question whether the label is worth the trouble. There is a second limit as well. Certified groups can produce far more coffee than fair-trade buyers want, so much of their crop is still sold at ordinary prices. Critics also ask how much of the extra money that shoppers pay actually reaches the farm. One study of coffee sold in Britain in the 1990s found that growers received only about 2 percent of the extra price paid in stores, while distributors in Britain kept a far larger share. A fair-trade label, then, is less a promise of wealth than a safety net, and it works best when prices fall.

options.B: It is paid to each farmer as extra personal income.

translation_zh.text:
在許多咖啡豆包裝上，消費者會看到一個小標籤，說明這些咖啡豆是以公平的方式交易的。這個標籤背後，是一個長久以來的擔憂。全世界大部分的咖啡由小型家庭農場種植，而這些農民拿到的價格每年都可能大起大落。例如在 2001 年 10 月，世界咖啡價格跌到每磅 45 美分的歷史低點，讓開發中國家各地的小農陷入困境。

公平貿易的設計就是為了緩和這類衝擊。要使用這個標籤，買家必須向組成合作社的農民購買咖啡，合作社是由成員以民主方式經營的團體。買家還必須至少支付一個最低價格，這個價格是根據以永續方式種植咖啡的估計成本訂定的。當市場價格高於這個底價時，就改用較高的市價。此外，買家同意建立長期的交易關係，而且在農民要求時預先支付部分貨款。

這項交易還包括一小筆稱為「溢價」（premium）的額外款項。它是給整個團體，而不是給任何一位農民的，成員會投票決定怎麼使用。常見的用途包括培訓、為成員提供的服務、提升品質的計畫，以及社區建設。

在 2001 年的危機中，這套制度證明了它的價值：公平貿易咖啡的價格比市價高出 180%。然而，當世界價格很高時，這個優勢就會縮小，有些農民便懷疑這個標籤是否值得那麼麻煩。還有第二個限制：取得認證的團體能生產的咖啡，遠多於公平貿易買家想買的量，所以大部分的收成仍然以一般價格出售。

批評者也質疑，消費者多付的錢究竟有多少真的到了農場。一項針對 1990 年代在英國銷售的咖啡所做的研究發現，種植者只拿到商店額外售價的約 2%，而英國的經銷商拿走的份額則大得多。如此看來，公平貿易標籤與其說是致富的承諾，不如說是一張安全網，而且在價格下跌時最能發揮作用。
